Bench-Seat Sleeper: 1967 Ford Fairlane Hides Dual-Quad Surprise Under the Hood
14 photos
Photo: Duffy's Classic Cars/eBay
Introduced as a full-size car in 1955 , the Fairlane was Ford's flagship model until the Galaxie arrived in 1959. In 1962, the Fairlane joined the emerging intermediate car market. Like most mid-size cars of the era, it also joined the muscle car wars.
As a bread-and-butter automobile, the Fairlane came standard with an inline-six engine, while the option list included an assortment of small-block V8 powerplants. In 1966, however, Ford added the 390-cubic-inch (6.4-liter) FE to the lineup. Additionally, the larger 427-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) V8 found its way under the Fairlane's hood for homologation purposes.
Rated at 425 horsepower, the R-code V8 was fitted into only 57 cars that year. While low, the number allowed Ford to homologate the powerplant (and the Top-Loader four-speed manual gearbox) for NHRA and IHRA Super Stock racing.
The following year, the Fairlane became available with the W-code 427, which featured a four-barrel carburetor and delivered 410 horsepower. However, the R-code engine remained on offer for customers who wanted to take the Fairlane racing. It's still unclear how many of these dual-quad factory race cars were built, but the consensus is that fewer than 100 left the assembly line.
These cars are obviously very desirable today, and one has recently surfaced in Cedar Rapids, Iowa. It's a fully restored example in Ivy Gold Green, and it's looking for its next caretaker.
I haven't seen many 1967 R-code cars on the auction block recently, so this hardtop is a pretty big deal. The fact that it looks like it just rolled off the assembly line is a big plus. Many of these cars were raced back in the day and then spent decades in long-term storage.
The metallic green paint looks gorgeous, while the chrome trim is flawless. If you're a fan of color-keyed interiors, this Fairlane delivers; the cabin has the same shade of green as the body, with dark green inserts on the seats. Speaking of which, this Fairlane 500 was equipped with a front bench seat. It also has the cheap steel wheels, so it's pretty much a sleeper.
But make no mistake though, this Fairlane is not your grandma's weekend rig. It still packs the 427 R-code and Top-Loader combo, which was quite expensive back in the day. Priced at $1,752.20, it added a 72% premium to the Fairlane's base sticker. The R-code went for over $4,000 at the time (that's more than $41,000 in 2026 dollars), which explains the low production number.
Speaking of which, the seller says this Fairlane is one of 72 units built with this drivetrain. Most sources, however, claim that Ford actually put together 92 examples. Typo or mistake aside, this R-code Fairlane is super rare, with fewer still in solid condition today.
The muscle car is being auctioned off by a dealership , and bidding has reached $50,300 with less than two days to go. The reserve is still in place, and I have a feeling that the seller is aiming for a six-figure sum.
